idiom_name: Flow.retry / retryWhen with a computed delay() in the predicate
implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines supplies the re-execution and the wait: `flow.retry(retries = n) { cause -> ... }` (or the general retryWhen, of which retry is documented as the shorthand) re-runs the upstream flow while the predicate returns true, and delay() suspends without blocking a thread and is cancellable, so the backoff honours coroutine cancellation instead of pinning a dispatcher thread. The schedule arithmetic (base, multiplier, cap, jitter) stays in your code or a small helper that the predicate calls. Use the operator rather than Thread.sleep, whose blocking behaviour ignores both cancellation and the dispatcher, and always bound retries because the operator's retries parameter defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE (retry forever).
code_sketch:
val payload = flow { emit(client.call()) }
    .retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
        if (cause !is IOException || attempt >= 5) return@retryWhen false
        val ceiling = minOf(30_000L, 200L shl attempt.toInt())
        delay(Random.nextLong(ceiling + 1))   // full jitter, cancellable and non-blocking
        true
    }
    .first()
pitfalls: retries defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE, so an unbounded Flow.retry keeps retrying forever; always pass an explicit bound and combine it with a time budget.
Thread.sleep inside a coroutine blocks the dispatcher thread and cannot be cancelled; delay() is the cancellable primitive.
A shared mutable attempt counter across concurrent flows corrupts the schedule - keep the state per call or use retryWhen's attempt parameter.
